Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette: The rain had turned the interstate into a sheet of black glass. Linh was driving home from a late shift at the tech campus when a deer materialized at the shoulder. She jerked the wheel, tires screamed, and the world inverted. Metal groaned, airbags deployed with a chemical bite, and for a long moment Linh lay pinned beneath the crumpled hood, listening to the steady drip of coolant and the distant, muffled shouts of passing drivers. She watched a man in a red jacket rush toward the wreckage, calling out a name over the wind—a sound that would later fracture her calm every time she heard similar names spoken in passing. The silence that followed the rescue was worse than the impact. She remembered the helplessness, the way her hands trembled uselessly against the dashboard while others worked to free her, and she has never forgiven herself for not doing more to stop what happened. That powerlessness calcified into a quiet conviction: if she had just driven slower, if she had paid closer attention, the collision would never have happened. She began carrying a heavy, unspoken verdict about her own actions, believing the crash was entirely her fault, and a corresponding suspicion that those who claimed to care were simply waiting for her to falter again. In the weeks that followed, the accident’s shadow lengthened across her daily routine. When her husband raised his voice during a disagreement about weekend plans, the sharp timbre of the argument sent her pulse racing until she had to excuse herself. The suddenness of those conflicts mirrored the chaos of the highway, and hearing similar names spoken in passing instantly resurrected the narrative that the collision was entirely her fault, reinforcing the suspicion that she could not rely on others. Because of those triggers, the dread they provoked pushed her to isolate, leading her to decline invitations and avoid any situation that placed physical demands on her body. Carrying that unspoken verdict about her own actions, she found herself avoiding friends and retreating to her home office, convinced that stepping forward would only expose her to more betrayal. Every time she chose withdrawal over connection or pressed her thumb into her palm until the sharp sting physically distracted her from the event, the negative appraisals deepened, making her believe she was fundamentally broken and that people would ultimately prefer her to step aside. The more she steered clear of physical exertion and social contact, the more isolated she became, which only magnified her sensitivity to uncertainty, turning ordinary scheduling conflicts into paralyzing threats. Over the next several months, these habits woven themselves into the architecture of her life. When her IT team scheduled a mandatory on-site server migration, the uncertainty of the deadline triggered a familiar tightening in her chest, leading her to avoid physical stress by requesting permanent remote work. She spent her days in a dimly lit apartment, managing databases behind a locked door where the only sounds were the hum of her monitors and the rhythmic tapping of her keyboard. Yet the isolation did not bring peace; instead, the withdrawal itself sharpened her focus on her own perceived failures. Every time she chose safety through distance or self-punishment, the negative appraisals deepened, making the next trigger feel sharper, more immediate, and impossible to outrun. Now, sitting in the waiting area of a trauma clinic, Linh clutched a referral slip until her fingers ached. She had come because the distance between her and the world had grown too wide to bridge alone, and because the quiet rituals she had built to survive the wreck were slowly eroding the life she still wanted. She feared that seeking help would force her to relive the impact, but she was equally afraid that if she did nothing, she would remain trapped in a loop of her own making, forever waiting for the other shoe to drop. What she hoped for, more than she dared say aloud, was a way to quiet the self-blame, to trust that she could navigate uncertainty without breaking, and to finally feel safe in her own body again.
